clue.text: State of shock from upset in sport, United being held

indicators.note: whatever is being held sits inside the grip of something else, so one piece goes within another
something upset is knocked over and thrown into disorder, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
U is the standard abbreviation for United, as in football club names

explanation.surface: A football shock: a sporting upset with a United side left stunned.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange SPORT as ST-POR and slip U between the halves to get STUPOR.
explanation.definitionFit: A stupor is a dazed, barely conscious condition, the kind brought on by severe shock.

clue.text: This needs two, little bit over zero

indicators.note: in a down entry one part placed over another simply comes first, ahead of what follows

parts.note: a tang is a slight trace or hint, as of a flavour
the letter O looks like the figure zero

explanation.surface: A sum of sorts: two of something, plus a little bit more than nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the saying 'it takes two to tango'.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says it takes two to tango, so this Argentine dance famously requires a pair of partners.

clue.text: In a mess, repulsive mill

indicators.note: things in a mess are jumbled up, so the letters come out in a scrambled order

parts.note: the nine letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A filthy, dilapidated old mill described as repulsive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mill' looks like a noun, a factory building, but it is the verb meaning to grind.
explanation.definitionFit: To mill grain is to grind it into powder, which is exactly what crushing something to dust means.

clue.text: Bear nipped by vultures is terrified

indicators.note: something nipped is caught between the jaws, so the word sits gripped inside the following words

parts.note: spans the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A bear gets pecked by vultures and is frightened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear' looks like the animal, but it is the verb meaning withstand or hold out against.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear pressure is to withstand it, and to withstand an attack is to stand firm against it.

clue.text: Where strikers found in penalty area at end of game

indicators.note: placed at the end of something means coming after it, so one piece follows the other

parts.note: a match is a game, as in a football match
football slang calls the penalty area the box

explanation.surface: Football: where the forwards are found at the end of a game, in the opposition's penalty area.
explanation.walkthrough: Strikers are not footballers here but matches, which strike to light; the box comes after the game.
explanation.definitionFit: Matches are things you strike, so the small container holding them is their home.

clue.text: Texan maniac, he'd set out to arrest leader from Cancun â steps taken there?

indicators.note: to arrest is to seize and hold, so one letter is kept inside the others
to set out is to lay things out afresh, so the letters are put in a new arrangement

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

indicators.note: the leader of a word is the one at the front, so only its opening letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the Mexican resort

explanation.surface: A crazed Texan sets off to apprehend a gang boss from Cancun.
explanation.walkthrough: The C from Cancun goes in among the other letters before they are all rearranged. 'There' points to the hat: the dancers step around a sombrero placed on the floor.
explanation.definitionFit: In this traditional folk dance the performers circle and step around a sombrero laid on the ground.

clue.text: Resolve shown, assigning same number to every metropolis?

parts.note: a number, the same one handed out to each
A means per or each, as in 'ten a day'
a metropolis is a large city

explanation.surface: Determination is needed to give every big city an identical figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Read it as 'ten a city': ten for each city, giving every metropolis the same number.
explanation.definitionFit: Resolve as a noun is firm determination, and tenacity is the quality of holding on stubbornly.

clue.text: Bird, another one missing a note!

indicators.note: what is missing has gone, so those letters are taken out

parts.note: the two words run together; that the result also runs unbroken inside them is a coincidence of trimming both ends
the letters to strip away: A and NOT at the front, E at the end

explanation.surface: Another bird has gone missing, a note left behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A note' looks like a musical note, but it is just the letters A, N, O, T, E: remove ANOT from the front and E from the end of ANOTHERONE.
explanation.definitionFit: The heron is a long-legged wading waterbird, a common example of the general category.

clue.text: Criminal allied with boy where justice sought

indicators.note: something criminal is crooked and bent out of line, so the letters are twisted into a new order

parts.note: first part of the letters to rearrange
second part of the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A crook teamed up with a young lad, in a place where justice is pursued.
explanation.walkthrough: The Old Bailey is the popular name of the Central Criminal Court in London, so 'Criminal' fits the scene as well as signalling the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: This famous London court tries serious crimes, so it is a place people go seeking legal redress.

clue.text: Inhabitant of ancient Britain, a long, woolly horn on

indicators.note: woolly means fuzzy and muddled, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
a saxophone is a horn in jazz slang
taken as written

explanation.surface: An early Briton pictured with long shaggy hair and a horn, like some Celtic warrior.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Woolly' and 'horn' suggest an animal such as a ram; in fact 'horn' is the musician's word for a saxophone.
explanation.definitionFit: The Anglo-Saxons were the Germanic peoples who settled in England after the Romans left, so early medieval inhabitants.

clue.text: Travel free, heading for Essex

parts.note: to rid is to free, as in rid of a burden

indicators.note: the heading of a word is the part at the top, so only its opening letter is used

parts.note: the first letter of the county

explanation.surface: A free trip out to Essex, the county just east of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Travel free' reads like a bus pass, but 'free' is the verb meaning to release.
explanation.definitionFit: To ride is to travel on a horse, bike or vehicle, so it works as a verb for journeying.

clue.text: Scattering of conifers related to investigative science

indicators.note: a scattering throws things about at random, so the letters land in a new order

parts.note: the eight letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Scattered pine needles examined by crime-scene experts.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's crime-scene flavour is apt: needles scattered at a scene are just what such scientists would study.
explanation.definitionFit: Forensic work applies scientific methods to gathering evidence for criminal investigation and courts.

clue.text: Is able to preserve cabaret entertainment

parts.note: can means is able to
to can food is to preserve it in a tin

explanation.surface: A performer manages to keep a nightclub act going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Preserve' sounds like keeping alive, but it is the kitchen sense of sealing food in a tin.
explanation.definitionFit: The high-kicking dance made famous at Parisian nightclubs like the Moulin Rouge is a classic stage show number.

clue.text: Legendary monster, strange being, one on peak in Yangra

indicators.note: the peak of a word is its top, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of the Himalayan mountain
ET, the film alien, is an extraterrestrial
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A legendary creature spotted on a Himalayan summit.
explanation.walkthrough: Yangra is a peak in the Nepal Himalaya, the yeti's home turf, and 'peak' doubles as the signal for a first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The yeti, or abominable snowman, is a mythical ape-like creature of Himalayan folklore.

clue.text: Choose mouth for sort of roll?

parts.note: to elect is to choose
oral means of the mouth

explanation.surface: Picking which way to roll something around in the mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is adjectival: the answer describes a kind of roll, not a roll itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The electoral roll is the official register of voters in Britain, so this word describes one particular list.

clue.text: Never my pleasure

definitions.meaning: first meaning: in no way, absolutely not
second meaning: the polite reply when someone says thank you

explanation.walkthrough: Read together, the two words sound like a snub; apart, they are a flat refusal and a gracious reply to thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase serves both as an emphatic negative and as a courteous response brushing off gratitude.

clue.text: One up for trial?

parts.note: surface reading: a defendant due to appear in court
setter's reading: someone up in the air flying a new aircraft to try it out

explanation.walkthrough: 'Up for trial' is the courtroom idiom; here 'up' means airborne and 'trial' means a test flight.
explanation.definitionFit: This professional flies experimental or new aircraft to evaluate their performance before general use.

clue.text: Defender's leg imparted effect on ball

parts.note: a back is a defender in football, and the apostrophe-s gives the S
pins is slang for legs

explanation.surface: A footballer's leg puts some swerve on the ball.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive 's is read as the letter S tacked onto the back.
explanation.definitionFit: Backspin makes a ball rotate against its direction of travel, a deliberate effect in tennis, golf or snooker.

clue.text: Something sweet and unusual recalled in extraordinary mead

indicators.note: to recall is to call back, so the word is taken backwards
in places one piece inside another
extraordinary means out of the ordinary, so the letters fall out of their usual order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
rare means unusual

explanation.surface: A sweet and unusual honey wine remembered as remarkable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Something sweet and unusual' wants to be one phrase; the definition stops at 'sweet'.
explanation.definitionFit: Demerara is a light brown cane sugar, named after a region of Guyana, so it is a sweetener.

clue.text: Very healthy ultimately, a type of protein

parts.note: so means very, as in 'so good'

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter counts

parts.note: the last letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A health-food claim: in the end, a particularly wholesome kind of protein.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very healthy' looks like one phrase but splits into SO and the last letter of the second word.
explanation.definitionFit: Soya beans are a major plant source of protein, used in tofu and meat substitutes.

clue.text: Shrub appearing cold, as climate is Arctic initially

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so the opening letter of each word is kept

parts.words: appearing cold, as climate is Arctic
parts.note: the opening letters of these six words

explanation.surface: A bush looking chilly, since the weather there is polar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appearing' looks like a link word joining definition to wordplay, but its first letter is needed too.
explanation.definitionFit: Acacia is a genus of thorny trees and bushes, including the wattles of Australia and Africa.

clue.text: Small vehicle pranged

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a truck is a vehicle

explanation.surface: A little car got dented in a crash.
explanation.walkthrough: To prang is British slang for crashing or damaging a vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: Pranged means hit in a collision, so the past tense of strike fits the same sentence.

clue.text: Dairy product skimmed, say

indicators.note: skimming takes the top layer off, so the word loses its first letter

parts.note: butter is made from cream

explanation.surface: Skimmed milk, for instance, as a low-fat dairy product.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skimmed' suggests skimmed milk, and 'say' looks like 'for example'; in fact the top letter comes off and 'say' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To utter something is to speak it aloud, a straightforward synonym for the verb.

clue.text: Crack hard to find in freshly pierced shell?

indicators.note: to be found in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within another
a shell is an outer casing, so these letters wrap around what goes inside
freshly means anew, so the letters are made up again in a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A crack in a shell that has just been pierced is hard to spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack' looks like a noun for a fissure; it is the verb, as in cracking a code. 'Shell' pictures the rearranged letters as a casing round the H.
explanation.definitionFit: To crack a code or cipher is to work out its meaning, which is what decoding it means.

clue.text: Colour that is uplifting in duck

indicators.note: in a down entry lifting up turns the letters bottom to top, so they read backwards

parts.note: red is a colour
i.e. is the abbreviation for that is

explanation.surface: A cheerful touch of colour on a duck.
explanation.walkthrough: RED and IE are joined, then the whole string is turned upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: The eider is a large sea duck whose soft breast feathers give eiderdown.

clue.text: Brood in ferment, oddly

indicators.note: oddly points to the odd-numbered positions, so first, third, fifth and seventh letters are kept

parts.note: the odd-placed letters of the word

explanation.surface: A family of young creatures in an odd state of agitation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brood' looks like a noun for a hatch of chicks; it is the verb meaning to worry.
explanation.definitionFit: To brood is to dwell anxiously on something, and to fret is likewise to worry persistently.

clue.text: Drink in a company car required by first of passengers

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, so only that is taken

parts.note: the first letter of the word
taken as written
taken as written
CO is the abbreviation for company
Lada is a Russian make of car

explanation.surface: Having a drink in the firm's car, as demanded by the passengers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drink in' looks like a phrase; the definition is only 'Drink' and 'in' is part of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A pina colada is a cocktail of rum, coconut cream and pineapple juice.

clue.text: Peer briefly through barrier, viewing Italian city

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the final letter is dropped
something seen through an enclosure is within it, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: a fence is a barrier
a lord is a peer, cut short by one letter

explanation.surface: Someone peeps through a fence for a quick look at an Italian city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer' looks like the verb to look closely; it is the noun, a member of the nobility.
explanation.definitionFit: Florence is the Tuscan capital and Renaissance art centre, one of the best known cities in Italy.

clue.text: Cast, cast or cast!

indicators.note: to cast is to throw, and thrown letters land in a new arrangement

parts.note: the six letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: One word repeated three times, like a stage direction or a fishing instruction.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word does three jobs: the first is the definition, the second is anagram material with 'or', and the third signals the shuffle by its sense of throwing.
explanation.definitionFit: A cast is the company of performers in a play or film, so the players collectively.
